Sliding Doors

The Mazda5 was the right car in the wrong timeline. Twenty years later the doors have opened again — and this time you can afford to step through.

By Priya Raghavan · 20 min read

There is a 1998 movie in which a woman's entire life forks on whether she makes it through a closing subway door. Same woman, same city, same ambitions. One version of her catches the train and everything changes. The other watches the doors shut in her face and spends the film living a smaller, slower, more disappointing story. Nothing about her is different in either timeline. Only the timing is.

I have been thinking about that movie a lot lately, because I keep running into Mazda5s.

One van, one door, two timelines. In 2006 it stayed shut while the crossovers went by. In 2026 it slides all the way back — and the ticket costs a third of what it did.

Every so often the industry produces a vehicle that fails not because the idea was bad, but because nobody quite knew what to do with the idea at the moment it arrived. The Mazda5 was one of those cars. Or vans. Or wagons. And there, in three nouns and a shrug, you have essentially explained its entire commercial problem.

What exactly was it? Mazda called it a "multi-activity vehicle," which is the kind of phrase that gets approved in a conference room and dies in a showroom. Journalists called it a mini-minivan, a microvan, a tall wagon and occasionally a crossover.

The truth is the Mazda5 wore a lot of hats. Family van on Monday, cargo hauler on Wednesday, canyon-road hatchback on Sunday, camper in August. The trouble with a car wearing five hats is that it is nearly impossible to sell to someone who walked in looking for one. But note carefully what it was not. It was not a jack of all trades and master of none. It was a genuine master of several of them — it just refused to name which one it wanted to be judged on.

Master of some. Not none.The line Mazda's marketing never found

And yet here is the strange part. Nearly twenty years after it landed in America, the Mazda5's formula reads less like a failure and more like a spec sheet somebody would write today, on purpose, hoping it goes viral. Six seats. Two sliding doors. About 180 inches long and 69 inches wide. A turning circle that doesn't require three ZIP codes. A Mazda3-derived chassis with an independent multilink rear suspension. An available manual transmission. Room to swallow bicycles, camping gear, surfboards or a week's worth of family detritus.

The specification that matters most, though, is the one Mazda never printed: today you can buy one for the price of a moderately irresponsible trip to Costco.

I've driven these things, and the part the spec sheet fails to communicate is that they are fun. Not "fun for a minivan," which is the automotive equivalent of "great personality." Actually fun. You sit higher than you would in a Mazda3 and there is considerably more air behind you, but underneath it all is a surprising amount of the old Zoom-Zoom Mazda. The steering talks to you, the chassis wants to change direction, the thing feels light on its feet, and you can see out of it in every direction. Then you arrive somewhere, slide open two enormous doors, and discover that the little machine you just hustled down a canyon road will carry six people.

The Mazda5 may be the best example we have of America buying the vehicle it wanted instead of the vehicle a lot of families actually needed. And now that everyone has forgotten it existed, it has quietly become one of the most interesting bargains on the American used market.

The doors are open again. They will not stay open forever.

01 — The premiseThe idea was almost aggressively sensible

The Mazda5 arrived in the United States for the 2006 model year, and internationally the concept wasn't remotely revolutionary. Compact people movers had existed for decades in Japan and Europe, where narrow streets, expensive fuel and impossible parking made enormous vehicles a form of self-punishment.

America was different. Our minivans had spent twenty years getting bigger. The original Dodge Caravan had been a tidy, sensible family device; by the mid-2000s the American minivan had become a rolling living room. Odyssey, Sienna, Town & Country — fantastic vehicles, all of them, and all enormous.

Mazda went the other way, and the numbers are more startling than the story usually gets credit for.

Overall length, in inches
Odyssey '12202.9

CX-5 '13179.3
Caravan '84175.9

Bars measured from a 160-inch baseline, because plotted from zero these all look identical and the whole point is the gap. the Mazda5 the crossover that replaced it context.

Look at what that chart is actually saying. The Mazda5 was nearly two feet shorter than the vans it was sold alongside — and only four and a half inches longer than the 1984 Caravan that invented the entire American minivan, while being a fraction narrower. It was never a miniature minivan. Minivans had become enormous, and the Mazda5 was simply the size a minivan used to be.

Then there's that amber bar. The first-generation CX-5, the crossover that would go on to eat the Mazda5's lunch inside Mazda's own showroom, was shorter than the Mazda5 and three and a half inches wider — with one fewer row and two fewer seats. America didn't switch to the CX-5 because it was bigger or more capable. America switched because of what it looked like it might do on a weekend.

Into that compact footprint Mazda packaged three rows, six seats and two sliding doors, arranged 2+2+2: two up front, two captain's chairs in the middle, two in the back, and no miserable middle passenger anywhere in the vehicle. That was a genuinely upscale idea at the time — the same seating architecture you'd find in a Chrysler Pacifica or a Mercedes-Benz R-Class — dropped into a van aimed at young families who were never going to spend Mercedes money.

Better still, it wasn't built on some agricultural commercial-van platform with a bench bolted in. Underneath was Mazda3 DNA, and that distinction turns out to matter enormously.

02 — The chassisA minivan that didn't drive like one

The Mazda5 shared its engineering philosophy with the Mazda3, including an independent multilink rear suspension. On paper that reads like a footnote. On a back road it is the entire story.

Car and Driver found that the 5's controls and responses worked together so naturally that it was actually enjoyable to wring out, which is not a sentence anyone has ever written about a Sienna. Their 2012 automatic tester pulled 0.81 g on the skidpad and hit 60 mph in nine seconds flat. Edmunds measured 0.80 g and a 63.7-mph slalom, noted the little van was quicker in a straight line than the Mazda2 they'd just tested, and concluded that it was simply fun to drive.

Nine seconds is not fast. But speed was never what made this thing entertaining. The steering is quick enough that the van feels eager to turn in, the body moves without lumbering, and the narrow track makes it absurdly easy to place. It behaves like a tall hatchback that happens to have a very large trunk with people in it.

That character is even more obvious in one particular version, because — and I want to be clear that this actually happened, in America, at a Mazda dealership — the Mazda5 was available with a manual transmission. The first-generation Sport came with a five-speed. The 2012 through 2014 Sport could be ordered with a six-speed stick.

Car and Driver took one of those six-speed cars to 60 mph in 8.3 seconds, a full seven-tenths quicker than the automatic, praised its precise steering and neutral handling, and called it the ultimate dad van.

It had no business being this entertaining.The Mazda5, in one line

03 — The flawExcept it needed more power, and it still does

Here comes the inevitable "but," because everyone who drives one arrives at the same thought within about four miles: this would be fantastic with another forty or fifty horsepower.

The original 2.3-liter four made 157 horsepower and 148 lb-ft — and then, in one of the great deflating asterisks of the era, the rating dropped to 153 horsepower for 2007 through 2010. The first-generation car got slower on paper without changing a single component.

The 2012 redesign brought a 2.5-liter four, which surely fixed it. It made 157 horsepower. Again. Torque improved usefully to 163 lb-ft at 4,000 rpm, but this was still a 3,457-pound vehicle designed to carry six human beings and their possessions. Load four adults, two kids and a weekend's luggage and those 157 horses have a very long afternoon ahead of them. Edmunds flagged acceleration as a principal weakness from day one, and Autoblog reached the same verdict on the second-generation car: better off the line, but highway passing still requires an appointment.

Which is frustrating, because the chassis deserved so much more. Imagine a 200-horsepower Mazda5. Better, imagine the Mazdaspeed5 that never existed — turbocharged four, six-speed manual, north of 200 horsepower, sliding doors, three rows. Mazda could have built the most irresponsible school-run vehicle in the history of the school run. Instead they built a very good one and left the power on the shelf.

Hold onto this complaint. It is the only one in this entire article that time has not quietly fixed.

04 — The other timelineJapan got the Mazda5 America should have had

In Japan the car was sold as the Premacy, and Japan got something we did not: four-wheel drive. Not a rumor, not a concept, not a forum fantasy — Mazda built and sold it.

In 2005 Mazda introduced a Premacy using an Active Torque Control Coupling four-wheel-drive system derived from the Atenza, promoted specifically for stability on wet and snow-covered roads. When the next generation arrived they did it again: in August 2010 Mazda released a new four-wheel-drive Premacy in Japan, with a system that automatically varied torque between the axles and a switch letting the driver select front- or four-wheel drive.

So picture the American campaign that never ran. Mazda5 AWD. Six seats, sliding doors, a compact-car footprint, outstanding visibility, Mazda steering, snow capability. That is no longer a quirky little van; that is a Subaru alternative. That is a ski car, a Colorado car, a Vermont car, a Pacific Northwest adventure wagon. That is precisely the vehicle Americans spent the following fifteen years buying by the million — as long as it was shaped like a crossover.

Mazda already had the hardware. It never crossed the ocean.

And while we're cataloging what Japan got and we didn't: Mazda also built the Premacy Hydrogen RE Hybrid, a series hybrid whose generator was a hydrogen-burning rotary engine. In March 2009 Mazda became the first manufacturer in the world to commercially lease a hydrogen hybrid, delivering the first car to Iwatani Corporation that May, then to the city of Hiroshima, Hiroshima Prefecture and Yamaguchi Prefecture. It made roughly 148 horsepower and would run about 124 miles on hydrogen — double the range of the RX-8 Hydrogen RE — with a dual-fuel system that let it fall back to gasoline when, inevitably, there was no hydrogen anywhere.

Sit with that. There exists, in Japan, a rotary-powered Mazda5. It has sliding doors and a Wankel. Somewhere near Hiroshima there is a prefectural employee who commuted in the single greatest minivan ever conceived and probably complained about the seat fabric.

05 — The cultThe following you never saw, because it lived somewhere else

Here is the part of the story that almost never gets told in America, mostly because Americans decided this car was invisible.

Everywhere else, the Premacy became a genuine object of enthusiasm. In Japan it was regarded highly enough that Nissan paid Mazda to sell it as their own: from June 2011 the Nissan Lafesta Highway Star was a Premacy with a restyled nose, flatter door panels and a Nissan badge, sold exclusively in Japan under an OEM agreement, right down to the same 2.0-liter direct-injection four. Taiwan got a version too — Ford Lio Ho, which assembled the Mazda5 locally, sold a rebadged one as the Ford i-Max from 2007 to 2011, following the first-generation Premacy that had been sold as the Ford Ixion. Four badges, one van. When the Premacy went out of production in February 2018, the Lafesta died a month later, because there was nothing underneath it anymore.

Then there's the modifying culture, which in Japan treats vans as a legitimate canvas rather than an admission of defeat. Japanese vanning (バニング) has been running since the late 1970s, and its VIP branch takes minivans and gives them the full treatment: slammed suspension, wide aftermarket wheels, rebuilt leather interiors, bodywork smoothed and lowered until a family hauler looks like a sedan that ate another sedan. Every January at the Tokyo Auto Salon, custom vans and kei vans sit under the lights on equal footing with tuned sports cars, and nobody snickers.

In Southeast Asia the Premacy grew a proper grassroots scene. Malaysia had an active Premacy club running gatherings, group buys and shared parts pricing down to the ringgit for brake pads and engine mounts — and, being enthusiasts, threads about which standalone ECU you'd want if you were going to turbocharge the thing. Facebook groups still span Premacy and Mazda5 owners worldwide, trading the hard-won knowledge of people who own a car its manufacturer stopped thinking about a decade ago.

America got the same vehicle and treated it as an appliance. The rest of the world got the same vehicle and threw it a party.

06 — The timingAmerica had already fallen in love with something else

The Mazda5 landed at exactly the wrong moment in the American psyche, and this is where the timing argument becomes unanswerable.

The minivan had once been the smartest thing in the driveway. Then it became uncool — an admission, a surrender, a public declaration that your interesting years were behind you. SUVs became aspirational, crossovers followed, and people started buying vehicles that suggested mountains and trailheads even when the week's most demanding expedition was a Trader Joe's parking lot.

The Mazda5 could not sell that fantasy, because it had sliding doors, and sliding doors are brutally honest. A crossover says perhaps this weekend we'll go kayaking. A minivan says I have Goldfish crackers under the second-row seat. Mechanically the gap between them was often trivial. Psychologically it was the Grand Canyon.

So the Mazda5 arrived asking Americans to admit something most weren't ready to admit: that they probably didn't need an SUV. That is a difficult proposition even when a company commits to it, and Mazda never really did. Car and Driver pointed out that the 5 received almost no marketing support at all — which is how you end up with a car even its own manufacturer struggled to describe. When the company can't explain what a vehicle is, the customer has no chance of explaining to their spouse why they bought one.

07 — The squeezeAnd Mazda was busy becoming a different company

There's a second timing problem layered under the first, and it's almost poignant.

Mazda itself changed enormously during the Mazda5's American life. The early car belonged to peak Zoom-Zoom Mazda — Mazda3, Mazda6, RX-8, MX-5, a company with a rotary halo and a chip on its shoulder. The second-generation car arrived wearing Nagare, the flowing wave-inspired design language, and was essentially the only vehicle that ever fully committed to it.

Then Mazda changed direction again. SKYACTIV became the engineering story, KODO became the design language, and the CX-5 arrived and immediately became the company's future. The Mazda5 suddenly looked like a product from a previous Mazda, and its drivetrain missed the company's single biggest technological transformation. Japan eventually got SKYACTIV-equipped Premacy variants; the American car never received the full treatment and soldiered on with an MZR four whose architecture traced back to 2001.

The math got brutal fast. In 2008 the Mazda5 accounted for 8.3 percent of Mazda's American volume. By 2014, Mazda was selling roughly seven CX-5s for every Mazda5. The car that killed it wasn't a Honda. It was parked at the other end of Mazda's own showroom.

For 2016, Mazda simply announced there were no plans to bring a replacement to the U.S. market beyond the 2015 model year. No farewell edition, no send-off, no eulogy. The strange little van just stopped.

Figures approximate; 2005 and 2006 confirmed against period reporting. 2005 and 2015 are partial-year bookends — the car went on sale in spring 2005 and ran out in 2015.

Its best year ever was 2008, at 22,021 vehicles. For perspective: while Mazda sold roughly 16,000 Mazda5s in 2010, Chrysler was moving about that many Town & Countrys every two months.

But look closer, because the shape of that chart says something more interesting than "it flopped." Sales didn't collapse. They wobbled along in the mid-teens for a decade, including a bump in 2011 and another in the redesign year. That is not the profile of a car that disappointed the people who bought it. That's the profile of a car that couldn't recruit new believers fast enough to replace the ones who moved on.

The Mazda5 wasn't failing its owners. It was failing to find enough of them.

09 — The verdictsThe critics were all saying the same thing

Go back through the contemporary road tests and a pattern emerges that has nothing to do with the car and everything to do with us. The journalists weren't asking Mazda to fix the Mazda5. They were asking Americans to reconsider what they actually needed.

Edmunds said buyers who wanted utility without surrendering carlike maneuverability should strongly consider it. Autoblog, writing in 2011 as Honda, Toyota and Nissan pushed their vans toward $40,000 and called it a family spa day, asked what you were supposed to buy if you wanted something small, efficient and inexpensive — something more like the original Caravan — and answered its own question: right now, there is only one choice on the market.

Autoblog ultimately called it perhaps the best family hauler available for under $20,000. That is a remarkable compliment for a car almost nobody remembers.

10 — The auditThe missed-opportunity ledger

The Mazda5 failed on four counts. Time has since reversed three of them. Here is the honest accounting.

Charge
Then · 2006–2015
Now · 2026
Marketing
FatalMazda couldn't explain the car, ran almost no advertising, and reached for a phrase — "multi-activity vehicle" — that has never once moved a human being toward a showroom.
IrrelevantNobody markets a fourteen-year-old used car to you. There is no campaign standing between you and a Mazda5 — just a listing, a price and a phone number.
Timing
FatalIt arrived mid-crossover-boom, asking buyers to accept sliding doors at the exact cultural moment when sliding doors read as capitulation.
PerfectVan life is a category. Micro-camping is a category. City parking got worse, not better. A whole generation now treats "the car I sleep in on weekends" as a purchase criterion.
Size
LiabilityAmericans in 2008 read compact as cheap. Two feet shorter than a real van sounded like two feet less car.
The pointIt fits a normal parking space, clears a garage height bar, and still swallows 44.4 cubic feet. The thing that killed it is now the first line of the pitch.
Power
Real flaw157 hp hauling 3,457 pounds and six people. Merging took planning. Passing took faith.
Still a flawThe one charge that never aged into a virtue. It softens — 65 mph with a mattress in the back and no meeting to reach is a different job — but it does not disappear.

Three out of four. In the other timeline — the one where the doors opened at a different moment — that's a hit.

11 — The openingAnd now comes the good part

Depreciation has done something wonderful to this car: it has stripped away every expectation. Nobody buys a Mazda5 because it's fashionable. Nobody buys one to impress a neighbor. Nobody stands next to one at Cars & Coffee discussing investment-grade provenance. You buy one because you look at the shape of it and think, hold on — what can this thing actually do?

Averages are asking prices and move by market; the floor is a running car with a hard life. KBB has the 2015 Sport down only 17 percent over three years — this curve has flattened, and some metros are ticking up.

That flattening is the number worth staring at. The Mazda5 is done falling. Which changes the whole equation, because you are no longer comparing it against a new crossover — you're comparing it against everything else that costs seven grand. And at seven grand, against high-mileage sedans and tired compact SUVs, a six-seat, sliding-door, multilink-rear-suspension Mazda that handles like a tall hatchback starts looking less like a used car and more like an exploit.

12 — The buildThe $7,000 beach house

This is my favorite thing to do with one, and it takes a weekend. Find a clean Mazda5. Pull or fold the rear seats, build a simple sleeping platform, add storage bins underneath, cut some window shades, throw in a cooler and a portable power station. Maybe a small roof box and board racks up top. Leave a towel permanently jammed behind the driver's seat, because it will end up there anyway.

Congratulations: you now own a tiny beach house with license plates.

And unlike a full-size camper van, you can actually park it — a distinction that grows more enormous the longer you live with it. A Sprinter conversion is wonderful until you need to parallel park it on a Friday night. A Transit build is fantastic until a garage posts a height restriction. The Mazda5 is 180.5 inches long, 68.9 wide and 63.6 tall: compact-car territory in every dimension, and shorter than plenty of midsize crossovers currently doing school runs.

Drop the third row and Mazda quoted 44.4 cubic feet. Fold the second row too and you're near 71 cubic feet with a nearly flat floor and 108 inches of wheelbase underneath it. Is it a Winnebago? Obviously not. That is precisely the point.

Van life, minus the second mortgage

Van life got enormous, and then van life got expensive. People now spend $50,000, $80,000, sometimes north of $120,000 turning cargo vans into mobile apartments with induction cooktops and satellite internet.

The Mazda5 proposes something simpler and, I'd argue, more honest. You don't live in it. You live out of it. Drive somewhere, sleep inside, wake up, slide open a door and you're outside — a beach, a trailhead, a campground, a festival, a national park, the parking lot of a bike race at 6 a.m. It isn't a motorhome. It's a bedroom that moves. And because it's fundamentally a compact car underneath, you aren't piloting a commercial vehicle for the other 350 days of the year when you just need to get to work.

The perfect second car for a couple

Leave the third row folded permanently and what you've built is a compact wagon with sliding doors and a big square cargo bay. You still have four genuinely usable seats. Friends visit, the third row pops up. Something needs moving, the seats disappear. You need to park downtown, and it's a non-issue. You need to load a dog, or a bike, or an ambitious Marketplace purchase, while another car sits six inches away in the next space — and that's when you understand the real luxury here.

Sliding doors. Once you've lived with them, conventional rear doors start to look like something the industry only tolerates out of habit.

And for a young family, better still

Two small children might be the Mazda5's perfect mission. Not five children, not three teenage linebackers. Two. Put them in the second-row captain's chairs, where they get their own armrests and cannot reach each other, which is worth more than any option package ever devised. The third row becomes emergency seating and stays folded, leaving a flat cargo area for strollers, bikes, beach gear, groceries, sports equipment, school bags and whatever sticky object a four-year-old has decided is essential that afternoon.

Because the van is narrow, nobody is wrestling a giant door open against the car parked alongside while holding a child seat. You slide, you load, you're done. That's the kind of mundane engineering that never makes an exciting commercial and improves your actual life every single day.

Be honest about the trade, though: behind the third row there's only about 5.5 cubic feet — roughly a row of grocery bags. Six people and their luggage do not fit in this vehicle simultaneously, and any owner who tells you otherwise is describing a trip they took once and did not enjoy.

13 — The buyWhich one would I choose?

I'd concentrate on the 2012–2015 generation: the 2.5-liter, standard stability and traction control, side and three-row curtain airbags, six seats, and the final evolution of the American car.

TrimWhat you get
SportThe simple one — and through 2014, the home of the six-speed manual
TouringFog lamps, Bluetooth, trip computer, 17-inch wheels, leather-wrapped wheel
Grand TouringLeather, heated front seats, xenon headlights, moonroof

If this were going to be my cheap beach-and-camping car, I'd hunt a 2012–2014 Sport manual — not because it's luxurious, but precisely because it isn't. It is the lightweight, inexpensive, six-speed, three-row Mazda van that should never have existed, and finding one now is a small act of historical preservation.

For a family daily driver, take a clean late-model Touring or Grand Touring automatic and don't think twice. At this age condition beats trim every time — a ratty Grand Touring is a worse purchase than an immaculate Sport, always.

What to look for

Start underneath, because rust matters more than anything else on this list, especially on cars that spent their lives in northern states. Inspect suspension mounting points, rocker panels, subframes, brake lines and the general underside. Then listen to the suspension: RepairPal lists front-suspension rattling from worn sway-bar bushings among the most commonly reported Mazda5 complaints, and owners have long reported uneven tire wear, so check all four corners rather than eyeballing tread depth on one.

Drive it over deliberately rough pavement and listen for clunks, rattles, wheel-bearing whine and suspension knock. Check the engine mounts, which produce noticeable vibration as they age. Test the air conditioning on a hot day if you can, because cooling a three-row cabin with compact-car HVAC hardware exposes weakness fast. Automatics should shift cleanly cold and warm. Manuals deserve a proper clutch inspection, partly because the sort of person who deliberately bought a manual minivan tended to understand exactly how entertaining that combination was.

Then work every mechanism in the vehicle, because this car is defined by its mechanisms. Both sliding doors. Every seat latch. Fold everything, unfold everything, tumble the second row, check the hidden under-seat bins, open and close the hatch.

And run the VIN. The recall that matters here is Mazda campaign 9916H, which began in April 2017 and covers 2012–2015 cars built between October 26, 2010 and June 22, 2015: the liftgate support struts can corrode, break, and drop the liftgate on whoever is standing under it. Earlier cars had their own campaigns, including power steering. A pre-purchase inspection is the best two hundred dollars you'll spend in this process.

Is it reliable?

Broadly yes, with the enormous qualification that the newest American Mazda5 is now more than a decade old. RepairPal rates it 4.0 out of 5 for reliability, with average annual repair and maintenance costs around $581 and a relatively low probability of severe repairs. Cars.com owner reviews for the 2015 car average 4.7 out of 5 — the sort of number you get when a vehicle's remaining owners are the ones who understood what they bought.

None of which makes every $4,000 Craigslist Mazda5 a smart purchase. Maintenance history matters. Rust matters. Accident history matters. A neglected 150,000-mile Mazda5 is still a neglected 150,000-mile automobile.

But there's nothing exotic here, and that is its own luxury. You're buying old-school Mazda mechanical simplicity — a naturally aspirated four, a conventional automatic or a cable-shifted manual, steel springs — rather than a depreciated luxury SUV stuffed with air suspension, twin turbos, electronically controlled everything and a repair estimate capable of ruining Christmas.

14 — The closeSliding doors

America eventually embraced almost everything the Mazda5 stood for. We decided we wanted smaller vehicles, better fuel economy, flexible interiors, carlike handling, compact crossovers, adventure vehicles, cars sized for cities, machines that could turn into camping platforms on a Friday afternoon. We built an entire social-media culture around exactly that.

The Mazda5 could do nearly all of it, twenty years ago, for less money than anything else on the road. We passed, because it looked too much like a minivan.

In the movie, the woman who misses the train doesn't get a worse life because she's a worse person. She gets a worse life because of three seconds of timing, and the film's whole ache is that she never learns the other version existed.

The Mazda5 is the car that missed the train. Same vehicle, same engineering, same six seats and sliding doors — dropped into 2006 instead of 2026. In the timeline where it arrives now, with all-wheel drive and forty more horsepower and a marketing department that calls it an adventure wagon instead of a multi-activity vehicle, it's a hit. Mazda sells every one they build to people in Denver and Burlington and Bend, the used ones command a premium, and there's a subreddit.

We got the other timeline. It was not the car's fault.

But here's what the Mazda5 offers that the movie never offers its heroine: the doors opened again. Not for Mazda — that ship sailed quietly in 2015, with no farewell edition. They opened for you.

Roughly $5,000 to $10,000 buys a decent one today. That isn't a cheap used car. It's cheap freedom. Throw a surfboard in the back. Take the kids to the beach. Fold everything flat and go camping. Move an apartment. Carry four friends. Take the dog somewhere. Buy an absurd piece of furniture from a stranger on the internet and actually get it home. Drive downtown and fit into a normal parking space when you arrive.

And when the road starts twisting on the way home, remember what's underneath you and enjoy yourself.

There aren't many vehicles that can do all of those things. There are far fewer that can do them for Mazda5 money. The Mazda5 wasn't the minivan America wanted. It may well have been the minivan America needed. We figured it out about fifteen years late — and the wonderful thing about being late is that it made the ticket cheap.

Mind the doors.They don't stay open
